notes: Slot 22 = Brazilian Armed Forces under Médici (ruling, MD sprite). The real civilian partner ARENA sits in slot 1 (pro-Western conservative, has popularity); coalition slot 13 holds Delfim Netto's technocrats of the 'economic miracle'. MDB moved from MD slot 15 to slot 2 (liberal-democratic legal opposition; oligarch slot does not fit 1970). Pro-Soviet PCB in slot 4, Maoist PCdoB in slot 19. ALN in slot 5; VPR and MR-8 referenced in its text since only one radical-left slot exists. FIESP in 15, CNBB in 14, House of Orléans-Braganza in 23 with MD sprite.

0.name: Serviço Nacional de Informações
0.text:
The National Information Service was created in June 1964 by General Golbery do Couto e Silva as the regime's intelligence agency. President Médici headed it before taking power, and under General Carlos Alberto da Fontoura it sits at the centre of a security apparatus hardened by Institutional Act No. 5.

The SNI embodies the national security doctrine taught at the Superior War College: total war against internal subversion, alignment with the United States and the West, and surveillance of every institution. It works alongside the army's hardline 'linha dura'. Its leverage is information, files on every politician and the power to recommend purges.

1.name: Aliança Renovadora Nacional
1.text:
The National Renewal Alliance was created in 1966, after the old parties were dissolved by Institutional Act No. 2, as the official party of the military regime. It gathers former members of the National Democratic Union, the Social Democratic Party and other conservatives, and it supports President Emílio Garrastazu Médici.

ARENA backs the regime's anti-communism, alignment with the United States, rapid economic growth and order. It is a party of governors, mayors and rural bosses who exchange loyalty for patronage. Its leverage lies in its majorities in Congress and the states, though real power remains with the generals.

2.name: Movimento Democrático Brasileiro
2.text:
The Brazilian Democratic Movement is the only legal opposition, created in 1966 under the regime's two-party system. Decimated by the purges that followed Institutional Act No. 5 in December 1968, it is presided over by Senator Oscar Passos, with Ulysses Guimarães among its leading figures.

The MDB calls for a return to the rule of law, direct elections, amnesty and respect for civil liberties, and criticizes the concentration of income behind the 'economic miracle'. It is a broad front ranging from liberals to former labourites. Its leverage is small but real: urban protest votes and the legitimacy of being the legal voice of opposition.

3.name: Partido Trabalhista Brasileiro
3.text:
The Brazilian Labour Party was founded in 1945 by Getúlio Vargas and became the party of João Goulart, the president overthrown in 1964. Dissolved in 1965, it survives as a tradition and a network in exile: Goulart lives on his ranches in Uruguay, and Leonel Brizola is confined there too.

Trabalhismo stands for labour rights, social security, agrarian reform, nationalization of strategic sectors and an independent foreign policy. Its old cadres now shelter inside the MDB. Its strength lies in the memory of Vargas among urban workers and in Rio Grande do Sul, where Brizola's name still carries weight.

4.name: Partido Comunista Brasileiro
4.text:
The Brazilian Communist Party, founded in 1922 and illegal for most of its history, follows the Soviet line under its veteran secretary-general Luís Carlos Prestes. Since 1964 it lives underground, and it has lost many of its most militant cadres to the armed groups.

The party rejects armed struggle and argues for a broad democratic front against the dictatorship, working inside the MDB, the unions and the universities. It supports Soviet foreign policy and peaceful coexistence. Its leverage lies in a disciplined clandestine organization, its intellectuals and its influence among journalists, artists and some labour leaders.

5.name: Ação Libertadora Nacional
5.text:
National Liberation Action is the largest urban guerrilla organization, founded in 1967 by Carlos Marighella after his break with the Communist Party. Marighella was killed in an ambush in São Paulo in November 1969, and Joaquim Câmara Ferreira now leads the organization, which cooperates with the MR-8 and Carlos Lamarca's VPR.

The ALN believes that bank raids, kidnappings and urban attacks will open the way to rural guerrilla war and the overthrow of the dictatorship. Its September 1969 kidnapping of US ambassador Charles Elbrick freed fifteen prisoners. It draws on students and Cuban training, but torture and informers are steadily destroying its networks.

6.name: TFP
6.native_full: Sociedade Brasileira de Defesa da Tradição, Família e Propriedade
6.text:
Tradition, Family and Property was founded in São Paulo in 1960 by the Catholic intellectual Plinio Corrêa de Oliveira. Its young members in red capes and lion standards campaign in the streets against agrarian reform, divorce and the progressive clergy.

The society defends a Catholic, hierarchical, counter-revolutionary order and rejects liberal modernity as much as communism; it views Vatican II reformers and the bishops' conference as traitors. Its leverage lies in its fanatical cadres, its petition drives with over a million signatures, and its ties to landowners and conservative officers.

7.name: A Ala Nacionalista
7.text:
The Nationalist Wing is the current of officers who rallied behind General Afonso de Albuquerque Lima, the former interior minister who sought the presidency in 1969 and was blocked by the high command. Its strength is among colonels and younger officers.

The wing wants the revolution of 1964 to serve national development rather than foreign capital: state control of minerals and energy, development of the Northeast and Amazon, and greater distance from Washington, as in Peru. It is as authoritarian as the regime, but anti-American in tone. Its leverage lies in barracks discontent and the prestige of its general.

8.name: Filhos de Jabal Amil
8.text:
The Sons of Jabal Amil are Lebanese Shia families in São Paulo, Paraná and the border trade around Foz do Iguaçu who follow Imam Musa al-Sadr, head since 1969 of the Supreme Islamic Shia Council in Beirut. They meet in homes and community halls rather than mosques.

They seek dignity for the Shia of south Lebanon and send remittances to their villages, while staying loyal to the Brazilian authorities. They distrust both superpowers. Their leverage is commerce, family networks spanning Brazil and Lebanon, and a growing presence in frontier towns.

9.name: Leitores de Najaf
9.text:
The Readers of Najaf are a tiny cluster of Shia immigrants in São Paulo who pass around the sermons of Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini, exiled in Najaf, where he has just lectured on government by the Islamic jurist. They have no premises and no public face.

They reject monarchy and secular nationalism and denounce both Washington and Moscow. Their horizon is revolution in Iran, not in Brazil. Politically they are invisible, but their fervour and links to the clerical networks of Iraq and Lebanon make them the seed of a militant movement.

10.name: Sociedade Beneficente Muçulmana
10.native_full: Sociedade Beneficente Muçulmana de São Paulo
10.text:
The Muslim Charitable Society of São Paulo was founded in 1929 by Syrian and Lebanese Sunni immigrants and built the Brazil Mosque on Avenida do Estado, the first mosque in Latin America. It is the central institution of Brazil's small Muslim community.

The society teaches orthodox, apolitical Islam, runs religious education and charity and cultivates links with Arab embassies and the Muslim World League. It is loyal to the Brazilian state and conservative in outlook. Its leverage lies in the wealth of Arab merchant families and its role as the community's voice.

11.name: Estudantes do Califado
11.text:
The Students of the Caliphate are a handful of Arab students in São Paulo who have encountered the pamphlets of Hizb ut-Tahrir, Taqiuddin al-Nabhani's party for the restoration of the caliphate. They meet in secret and number only a few dozen.

They regard every existing state as illegitimate and reject both capitalism and communism, calling for a single Islamic state under one caliph. In Brazil they are a curiosity, but their discipline and conspiratorial methods mirror those of the clandestine left around them on campus.

12.name: Irmãos da 25 de Março
12.text:
The Brothers of 25 de Março are Muslim traders from Syria, Lebanon and Palestine around São Paulo's Rua 25 de Março market who admire the Egyptian Muslim Brotherhood and Said Ramadan's exile network. They run Koran classes, charity and help for newcomers.

They want Islamic ethics in public and family life, solidarity with the Palestinian cause and independence from both blocs, while respecting Brazilian law. They avoid open politics. Their strength is a tight community of merchants and textile wholesalers in the heart of Brazil's largest city.

13.name: Os Meninos do Delfim
13.text:
Delfim's Boys are the young economists from the University of São Paulo gathered around Antônio Delfim Netto, finance minister since 1967 and the strongest civilian in Médici's government. They run the Finance and Planning ministries, the Central Bank and the development banks.

They promise the 'economic miracle': growth first, distribution later, with state investment, export incentives, wage controls and indexation. They care more about growth rates than ideology and court investors from every quarter. Their power comes from soaring GDP figures and the generals' need to legitimize the regime through prosperity.

14.name: Conferência Nacional dos Bispos do Brasil
14.english: National Conference of Bishops of Brazil
14.native_full: Conferência Nacional dos Bispos do Brasil
14.text:
The National Conference of Bishops of Brazil was founded in 1952 with Dom Hélder Câmara as its first secretary-general. Now Archbishop of Olinda and Recife, Dom Hélder is the regime's best-known critic abroad, while Dom Aloísio Lorscheider serves as secretary-general.

The conference speaks for the largest Catholic church in the world. Divided between conservatives and progressives inspired by Medellín, it increasingly denounces torture, poverty and land conflicts, while rejecting Marxism and violence. Its leverage lies in parishes reaching every village, base communities and the moral authority no general can silence.
14.wiki: National Conference of Bishops of Brazil

15.name: Federação das Indústrias do Estado de São Paulo
15.english: Federation of Industries of the State of São Paulo
15.native_full: Federação das Indústrias do Estado de São Paulo
15.text:
The Federation of Industries of the State of São Paulo, founded in 1931, represents the industrial heartland of Latin America. Its leaders backed the 1964 coup and are among the main beneficiaries of the boom now under way.

FIESP wants protection for domestic industry, cheap credit, wage restraint and a docile labour movement. Several of its members help finance Operation Bandeirante, the army's anti-guerrilla task force in São Paulo. Its leverage is enormous: capital, employment, the press it advertises in, and direct access to the finance minister and the generals.
15.wiki: Federation of Industries of the State of São Paulo

16.name: Instituto de Pesquisas e Estudos Sociais
16.english: Institute for Research and Social Studies
16.native_full: Instituto de Pesquisas e Estudos Sociais
16.text:
The Institute for Research and Social Studies was founded in 1961 by businessmen in Rio de Janeiro and São Paulo to fight Goulart's reforms. It financed propaganda and planning for the 1964 coup, and many of its associates, such as Roberto Campos, served in Castelo Branco's government.

IPES champions free enterprise, foreign investment, fiscal orthodoxy and integration into the Western economy, and distrusts the statism of the nationalist officers. Its influence has waned since 1967, but it remains a meeting place for liberal economists, bankers and multinational executives.
16.wiki: Instituto de Pesquisas e Estudos Sociais

17.name: Fundação Brasileira para a Conservação da Natureza
17.english: Brazilian Foundation for the Conservation of Nature
17.native_full: Fundação Brasileira para a Conservação da Natureza
17.text:
The Brazilian Foundation for the Conservation of Nature was founded in Rio de Janeiro in 1958 by naturalists, scientists and agronomists. It is the country's oldest conservation body and works with international organizations such as the IUCN.

The foundation calls for national parks, protection of the Atlantic Forest and the Amazon, and limits on hunting and deforestation, concerns sharpened by the regime's plans for highways into the rainforest. Its membership is small and scientific, but its contacts in ministries, museums and abroad give it a voice in conservation policy.

18.name: Ligas Camponesas
18.text:
The Peasant Leagues arose in Pernambuco in 1955 and, under the lawyer Francisco Julião, spread across the Northeast demanding land for sharecroppers and cane cutters. Crushed after the 1964 coup, they survive only in memory and scattered networks; Julião lives in exile in Mexico.

The Leagues stand for radical agrarian reform, an end to the sugar barons' power and dignity for rural workers, inspired by the Cuban revolution but independent of the communist parties. Their potential lies in the vast landless population of the Northeast, still waiting for the land the regime promised but never delivered.

19.name: Partido Comunista do Brasil
19.text:
The Communist Party of Brazil was reorganized in 1962 by João Amazonas, Maurício Grabois and Pedro Pomar, who broke with Prestes's pro-Soviet party. Clandestine and aligned with Peking and Tirana, it is quietly sending cadres to the Araguaia region in the Amazon.

The party rejects both Soviet revisionism and urban guerrilla adventurism, preparing instead a protracted people's war in the countryside on the Chinese model. Its leverage is a hardened clandestine leadership, a base among students and intellectuals, and a rural foothold the regime has yet to discover.

20.name: Os Lacerdistas
20.text:
The Lacerdists are the followers of Carlos Lacerda, the fiery former governor of Guanabara who helped topple Goulart in 1964 and then turned against the generals. His political rights were suspended in December 1968, and his Frente Ampla with Kubitschek and Goulart was banned.

Lacerdismo blends middle-class anti-communism, moral crusading, efficient administration and fierce oratory against corruption, while demanding elections the generals deny. It is pro-American and anti-populist yet itself populist. Its base lies in Rio's middle classes, and Lacerda's newspaper and voice remain formidable weapons.

21.name: Comando de Caça aos Comunistas
21.text:
The Communist Hunting Command is a far-right paramilitary group of students, policemen and off-duty officers that emerged in São Paulo in 1968. It became notorious for attacking the cast of the play 'Roda Viva' and for the battle of Maria Antônia street against leftist students.

The CCC preaches violent anti-communism, Christian nationalism and the extermination of subversion, acting with tacit protection from the security services. It has no programme beyond terror against the left, artists and progressive clergy. Its leverage lies in its links to the police and the hardline officers.

22.name: Forças Armadas Brasileiras
22.text:
The Brazilian Armed Forces have ruled since the coup of 31 March 1964. In October 1969, after President Costa e Silva's stroke and a brief junta, the high command chose General Emílio Garrastazu Médici, who governs with the sweeping powers of Institutional Act No. 5.

The military regime pursues security and development: elimination of the guerrillas through torture and censorship, alignment with the United States, and an economic boom it presents as proof of success. The officer corps is divided between hardliners and the 'Sorbonne' moderates, but united in its claim to guide the nation.

23.name: Casa de Orléans e Bragança
23.text:
The House of Orléans-Braganza is the imperial family of Brazil, deposed in 1889. Its Vassouras branch is headed by Prince Pedro Henrique, recognized by monarchists as head of the imperial house, while his cousin Prince Pedro Gastão of the Petrópolis branch disputes the claim.

The monarchists dream of restoring a Catholic constitutional empire as a symbol above party strife, an idea kept alive in genealogical societies and among the Catholic right. They have no organized party and no popular following. Their leverage is limited to prestige, history and sympathy among traditionalists.
